meaning: To wait idly for opportunities instead of taking initiative. To rely on chance or past luck rather than making an effort.
origin: A farmer in the State of Song saw a rabbit crash into a tree stump and die. He gave up farming and waited by the stump every day for more rabbits, becoming a laughingstock.
example_zh: 不要守株待兔，机会要靠自己去争取。
example_en: Don't just wait by the stump for a rabbit—go out and earn your opportunities.

meaning: To ruin something by adding unnecessary details. Doing extra work that ends up making things worse instead of better.
origin: In a drinking contest, the first man to finish drawing a snake added feet to his drawing to show off, and lost the prize to the second man who pointed out snakes have no feet.
example_zh: 报告已经很完善了，再加这些数据就是画蛇添足。
example_en: The report is already perfect; adding these extra figures is just drawing feet on a snake.

meaning: A person with a narrow worldview who thinks they know everything, unaware of the vast world outside.
origin: A frog living at the bottom of a well believed the sky was only as big as the opening of the well, until a sea turtle told him of the boundless ocean.
example_zh: 你没出过国，简直是井底之蛙。
example_en: You've never been abroad—you're like a frog at the bottom of a well.

meaning: To stubbornly hold onto outdated methods or ideas, ignoring that circumstances have changed.
origin: A man dropped his sword from a moving boat and carved a mark on the boat's side. When the boat stopped, he dove in where the mark was, but the boat had moved while the sword had not.
example_zh: 现在市场变了，你的旧策略就是刻舟求剑。
example_en: The market has changed—sticking to your old strategy is like carving the boat to find the sword.

meaning: To pursue a goal through completely wrong methods. Trying to achieve something in a way that can never work.
origin: Mencius told King Xuan of Qi that trying to rule the world through military force was like climbing a tree to catch fish—it would never succeed.
example_zh: 想靠买彩票致富，简直是缘木求鱼。
example_en: Hoping to get rich by buying lottery tickets is like climbing a tree to catch fish.

meaning: To waste one's words or efforts on someone who cannot understand or appreciate them. Talking over someone's head.
origin: A musician played beautiful music for a cow, but the cow only cared about eating grass—the music was wasted on a listener who couldn't understand it.
example_zh: 跟他讲哲学就是白费口舌，对牛弹琴。
example_en: Explaining philosophy to him is like playing the lute to a cow—a waste of breath.

meaning: To contradict oneself. Saying or doing things that cannot both be true at the same time.
origin: A man sold a spear that could pierce anything and a shield that nothing could pierce. When asked what would happen if the spear struck the shield, he had no answer.
example_zh: 你的话自相矛盾，无法自圆其说。
example_en: Your statements are self-contradictory—you can't have it both ways.

meaning: A loss may turn out to be a gain, and vice versa. Fortune and misfortune are interconnected and hard to judge in the moment.
origin: An old man on the frontier lost his horse. Neighbors consoled him, but he said 'How do you know this isn't a blessing?' The horse returned with a fine stallion. The story continues with fortunes reversing repeatedly.
example_zh: 没拿到offer别太难过，塞翁失马焉知非福。
example_en: Don't be too upset about not getting the offer—a loss may be a blessing in disguise.

meaning: It's never too late to fix a problem. Taking corrective action after damage has occurred is still worthwhile.
origin: A shepherd lost a sheep because his pen had a hole. His neighbor said it was too late to fix it, but the shepherd replied that fixing it now would prevent losing more sheep later.
example_zh: 虽然晚了，但亡羊补牢，为时未晚。
example_en: It's late, but better late than never—mending the pen after losing the sheep still helps.

meaning: To claim to like something but actually fear it when confronted with the real thing. Pretended affection that melts under reality.
origin: Lord Ye claimed to love dragons and decorated his whole house with dragon motifs. When a real dragon came to visit him, he was terrified and fled.
example_zh: 你说喜欢挑战，结果真遇到就跑了，真是叶公好龙。
example_en: You claim to love challenges, but run away when one actually appears—true Lord Ye loving dragons.

meaning: Perfectly done, with no flaws or gaps. Flawless execution or design.
origin: A heavenly weaver's garments had no seams, as they were woven from clouds—unlike earthly clothes made by human hands.
example_zh: 这个计划安排得天衣无缝。
example_en: The plan was arranged flawlessly, with no gaps.

meaning: Perseverance and determination can overcome seemingly impossible obstacles. Steady effort over generations accomplishes great things.
origin: An old man named Yu Gong decided to move two mountains blocking his doorway. Despite ridicule, he and his descendants dug daily, eventually moving the gods to pity, who sent angels to carry the mountains away.
example_zh: 只要坚持不懈，愚公移山也能成功。
example_en: With relentless persistence, even moving mountains is possible—the foolish old man's way.

meaning: The finishing touch that brings a work to life. A critical detail that elevates something from good to great.
origin: A painter painted four dragons on a temple wall but left out their eyes, claiming that with eyes they would fly away. Skeptics insisted, so he painted eyes on two—and they soared into the sky in a thunderstorm.
example_zh: 最后这句话是画龙点睛之笔。
example_en: This final sentence is the dotting of the dragon's eyes—the touch that brings it all to life.

meaning: To ruin something by rushing it. Trying to speed up a natural process and ending up destroying it.
origin: An impatient farmer pulled his rice seedlings upward to make them grow faster. He returned home exhausted but proud, only to find his seedlings withered the next day.
example_zh: 教育孩子不能拔苗助长。
example_en: Don't rush a child's education—pulling seedlings to help them grow only kills them.

meaning: An irresistible force or trend. Something so powerful that nothing can stand in its way.
origin: From classical military writings describing a victorious army's unstoppable momentum.
example_zh: 这股技术革命的浪潮势不可挡。
example_en: The wave of technological revolution is unstoppable.

meaning: Muddled thinking; to act without clear understanding. Living without purpose or awareness.
origin: From Chinese folk wisdom distinguishing '难得糊涂' (rare to be wisely confused) from foolish muddle.
example_zh: 他这事办得太糊涂了。
example_en: He handled this matter in a very muddled way.

meaning: To amaze everyone with a single brilliant act. Achieving sudden fame or success after a period of obscurity.
origin: King Zhuang of Chu was said to have been silent for three years before suddenly reforming the state and becoming a hegemon. A bird that doesn't fly for three years will soar to the sky when it finally does.
example_zh: 他这次比赛一鸣惊人，夺得冠军。
example_en: He stunned everyone by winning the championship—a single astonishing cry.

meaning: Beyond cure; a problem so deeply rooted it cannot be fixed. Originally referred to terminal illness.
origin: From the Zuo Zhuan: a doctor examined the Duke of Jin and declared his illness had entered the gao and huang regions (above and below the heart), where medicine could not reach.
example_zh: 这家公司的腐败已经病入膏肓。
example_en: The corruption in this company has reached the incurable stage.

meaning: To be in an extremely uncomfortable or anxious position. Feeling restless and uneasy.
origin: From the story of Du Xi in the Jin Dynasty, who was so upright that he felt like he was sitting on a needle mat when in the presence of corrupt officials.
example_zh: 等面试结果的时候，他如坐针毡。
example_en: Waiting for the interview result, he felt like he was sitting on a needle mat.

meaning: Very close by, within easy reach. Used to describe physical or figurative nearness.
origin: From classical literature describing proximity—the 'zhi' and 'chi' were ancient Chinese units of small distance (8 cun and 10 cun respectively).
example_zh: 机会就在咫尺之近。
example_en: The opportunity is within arm's reach.

meaning: To have an insatiable thirst for learning. Studying endlessly without growing tired of it.
origin: From the Analects of Confucius: 'To study and not be satiated, to teach and not grow weary—what difficulty is there in these for me?'
example_zh: 他一生学而不厌，著作等身。
example_en: He spent his life studying without satiation, and his writings equaled his height.

meaning: To rise early and work diligently. Seizing the morning to practice and improve oneself.
origin: Zu Ti and Liu Kun, friends in the Jin Dynasty, would rise at the first cockcrow to practice sword dancing, determined to serve their country.
example_zh: 他每天闻鸡起舞，刻苦训练。
example_en: He rises at the rooster's crow every day and trains diligently.

meaning: To burn one's bridges. Committing fully to a course of action with no retreat possible.
origin: At the Battle of Julu, Xiang Yu ordered his troops to sink their boats and smash their cooking pots after crossing the river, leaving them only three days of food—with no retreat, they fought to victory.
example_zh: 他破釜沉舟，辞职创业了。
example_en: He burned his boats—quit his job to start a business with no way back.

meaning: To accomplish the seemingly impossible through sheer will and effort. Transforming nature itself.
origin: From classical Chinese literature describing supernatural or heroic feats that alter the landscape.
example_zh: 我们有移山倒海的决心。
example_en: We have the determination to move mountains and overturn seas.

meaning: To recognize one's mistake but stubbornly refuse to correct it. Willful persistence in error.
origin: From folk wisdom criticizing those who, despite awareness of their wrongdoing, refuse to amend their ways.
example_zh: 知错不改是最大的愚蠢。
example_en: Knowing your mistake but refusing to change is the greatest foolishness.

meaning: To help others achieve their goals. To actively support another's success.
origin: From the Analects: 'The gentleman completes others' good, he does not complete others' bad. The small man does the opposite.'
example_zh: 我们应该成人之美，互相帮助。
example_en: We should help others succeed—completing their good.

meaning: To be fickle; changing one's mind or desires constantly upon seeing new things. Lack of steadfastness.
origin: From the Book of Rites, describing merchants who changed their wares whenever they saw something new.
example_zh: 他做事见异思迁，难以专注。
example_en: He's fickle in his work, unable to focus—always wanting to move on to the next new thing.

meaning: To weep alone in a corner, isolated from others' joy. Feeling left out while others celebrate.
origin: From a Han Dynasty story where a guest arrived late to a banquet and was placed facing the corner, weeping alone while others enjoyed the feast.
example_zh: 别一个人向隅而泣，加入我们一起庆祝吧。
example_en: Don't weep alone in the corner—join our celebration.

meaning: True qualities reveal themselves over time and through tests. Only through prolonged experience can one's true abilities or character be known.
origin: From the Song Dynasty, often paired with '日久见人心' (time reveals a person's heart).
example_zh: 路遥知马力，日久见人心。
example_en: A long road tests a horse's strength; time reveals a person's heart.

meaning: To grieve for someone whose fate might become your own. Feeling sorrow for the misfortune of a similar person.
origin: From the Yuan Dynasty novel 'Water Margin,' where outlaws grieved for a fallen comrade.
example_zh: 看到同行倒下，他难免兔死狐悲。
example_en: Seeing a fellow entrepreneur fail, he couldn't help but grieve—the rabbit dies, the fox weeps.

meaning: A person capable of leading many. One who has the ability to command and guide a large group.
origin: From classical military organization, referring to a commander who could lead a thousand soldiers.
example_zh: 他天生是千人之长的料。
example_en: He's a natural-born leader of thousands.

meaning: To attempt the impossible overnight. Expecting instant success without the necessary gradual process.
origin: From folk wisdom mocking those who expect unrealistic shortcuts.
example_zh: 创业没有一步登天的事。
example_en: There's no such thing as one-stepping to heaven in business.

meaning: Very clearly and distinctly. Without any doubt or ambiguity.
origin: From classical vernacular literature emphasizing vivid clarity.
example_zh: 他把事情看得真真切切。
example_en: He saw the matter very clearly and distinctly.

meaning: Persistent effort overcomes the hardest obstacles. Small actions repeated continuously accomplish great things.
origin: From a Song Dynasty judicial case where a clerk's small daily thefts added up to a fortune—like water drops eventually piercing stone.
example_zh: 坚持学习，水滴石穿。
example_en: Persist in studying—water drops eventually pierce stone.

meaning: Dumbfounded, completely speechless with shock or astonishment.
origin: From Yuan Dynasty drama describing characters struck speechless.
example_zh: 这个消息让他目瞪口呆。
example_en: The news left him dumbfounded—eyes staring, mouth hanging open.

meaning: To feel at home anywhere in the world. To live freely without being tied to one place.
origin: From the Book of Han, originally describing the emperor's dominion over all the world.
example_zh: 他常年出差，四海为家。
example_en: He travels constantly for work, making the four seas his home.

meaning: To proceed in an orderly, step-by-step manner. Following a planned sequence without rushing.
origin: From classical literature about official selection and procedure, meaning to follow established order.
example_zh: 项目要按部就班地推进。
example_en: The project should proceed step by step, in proper order.

meaning: Unknown to the public; living without fame or recognition.
origin: From classical literature describing those who lived quietly without renown.
example_zh: 他在小镇默默无闻地过了一辈子。
example_en: He lived his whole life in the small town, unknown to the world.

meaning: To know when to stop before going too far. To stop at the right moment.
origin: From the Analects of Confucius, advising moderation and restraint.
example_zh: 玩笑要适可而止，别太过分。
example_en: Jokes should stop where enough is enough—don't go too far.

meaning: The student surpasses the teacher. Successive generations improve upon their predecessors.
origin: From Xunzi: 'Indigo dye comes from the indigo plant, but is bluer than the plant itself.'
example_zh: 徒弟青出于蓝而胜于蓝。
example_en: The apprentice has surpassed the master—bluer than the indigo plant he came from.

meaning: To focus on trivial matters while neglecting the essential. To lose sight of what's truly important.
origin: From the Book of Han, describing agricultural neglect in favor of commerce.
example_zh: 注重包装而忽视质量，就是舍本逐末。
example_en: Focusing on packaging while neglecting quality is abandoning the root for the branches.

meaning: A wide variety; many different kinds of things. Diverse and colorful.
origin: From ancient tactical formations—the 'Five Flowers' and 'Eight Gates' were military formations that later came to represent variety.
example_zh: 市场上的商品五花八门，让人眼花缭乱。
example_en: The variety of goods in the market is dazzling—all sorts of things.

meaning: To hit the nail on the head with a single sentence. To reveal the truth in one incisive remark.
origin: From classical vernacular literature.
example_zh: 他一语道破了问题的关键。
example_en: He broke through to the heart of the matter with a single sentence.

meaning: To bring back from the brink of death. To save a hopeless situation miraculously.
origin: From stories of legendary physicians like Bian Que whose treatments seemed to revive the dead.
example_zh: 这位医生有起死回生之术。
example_en: This doctor has the skill to raise the dead and return life.

meaning: To find new life or opportunity after a period of decline. A second chance at success.
origin: From Buddhist scriptures, where the withered tree blossoming symbolized revival.
example_zh: 退休后他创业成功，枯木逢春。
example_en: After retirement, he started a successful business—dead wood meeting spring.

meaning: In the prime of youth, full of talent and vitality. At the peak of one's powers.
origin: From Mao Zedong's poem 'Qin Yuan Chun - Changsha' describing young revolutionaries.
example_zh: 他们风华正茂，正是干事业的好年纪。
example_en: They are in the prime of youth—the perfect age to build their careers.

meaning: Widely successful or flourishing everywhere. Proliferating successfully across many areas.
origin: From classical poetry describing abundant blooming.
example_zh: 这家公司分店花开遍地。
example_en: This company's branches have bloomed all over the place.

meaning: To become even more powerful. Adding strength to something already strong.
origin: From the Three Kingdoms period, describing Zhuge Liang joining Liu Bei's forces.
example_zh: 有了这笔投资，公司如虎添翼。
example_en: With this investment, the company is like a tiger with added wings.

meaning: The persuasive power of parables and stories. Teaching through narrative.
origin: Coined term referring to the rhetorical tradition of using parables like Zhuangzi's works.
example_zh: 寓言之力胜过千言万语的说教。
example_en: The power of parables outweighs a thousand words of preaching.

meaning: What is naturally appropriate to local conditions. Adapting to the environment.
origin: From classical Chinese philosophy on adapting to local geography and conditions.
example_zh: 做事要地道之宜，因地制宜。
example_en: Act according to what fits the local ground—adapt to conditions.

meaning: Rich, varied, and colorful; describing content, activities, or life as being full of variety and interest. It conveys a sense of abundance and diversity that makes something vibrant and engaging. Often used to praise events, cultures, or experiences as multifaceted and stimulating.
origin: The phrase is a modern compound idiom formed from the adjectives '丰富' (abundant, in use since classical times) and '多彩' (colorful, appearing in Tang and Song poetry). Unlike many chengyu tied to a single classical anecdote, it emerged as a fixed four-character expression in early 20th-century vernacular Chinese (baihua) literature, gaining widespread currency in newspapers and essays of the Republican era. It crystallized a long-standing aesthetic ideal in Chinese culture—valuing multiplicity and ornamentation—into a concise expression. Today it is one of the most frequently used descriptive chengyu in modern Chinese.
example_zh: 这个夏令营的活动丰富多彩，孩子们每天都过得很充实。
example_en: The summer camp offers a rich and colorful variety of activities, and the children have a fulfilling time every day.

meaning: Literally 'to open the door and see the mountain,' this idiom means to come straight to the point without beating around the bush. It describes speech or writing that is direct, candid, and gets to the heart of the matter from the very start.
origin: The phrase originates from Tang Dynasty poetry criticism, particularly associated with the poet and critic Yan Yu (严羽) in his work 'Canglang's Remarks on Poetry' (《沧浪诗话》). He praised poems that began directly with their main subject, like opening a door to immediately behold a mountain before one, rather than circling with ornamental preambles. The image reflects the Chinese aesthetic of clarity and directness in literary expression. Over time it became a widely used metaphor for straightforward communication in both writing and conversation.
example_zh: 他一进门就开门见山地说出了自己的来意。
example_en: As soon as he walked in, he came straight to the point and stated his purpose.

meaning: Describes earnestly and repeatedly seeking out talent or a wise person with great sincerity and humility. It conveys a leader's persistent effort to recruit someone valuable, even at personal inconvenience. Today it is used whenever someone makes repeated, sincere efforts to invite or win over an expert.
origin: The idiom comes from the late Eastern Han Dynasty, just before the Three Kingdoms period. The warlord Liu Bei, eager to restore the Han, learned that the brilliant strategist Zhuge Liang was living in seclusion in a thatched cottage at Longzhong. Despite winter weather and the objections of his brothers, Liu Bei personally called on Zhuge Liang three times before the recluse finally agreed to meet him and lay out the famous Longzhong Plan. Deeply moved by such humility, Zhuge Liang agreed to serve Liu Bei and became his chief strategist, helping found the state of Shu Han. The story is recorded in 'Records of the Three Kingdoms' (Sanguozhi) and later dramatized in 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms' (Sanguo Yanyi).
example_zh: 为了请到这位顶尖工程师，公司总经理三顾茅庐，亲自飞到外地登门邀请。
example_en: To recruit this top engineer, the company's CEO visited him in person out of town three times, like Liu Bei seeking out Zhuge Liang.

meaning: An idiom describing something of tremendous impact, scale, or intensity — literally earth-shattering. It is used for events, achievements, sounds, or actions so powerful that they seem to shake the heavens and the earth, leaving a profound impression on everyone who witnesses them.
origin: The phrase is classically traced to the Tang dynasty poet Bai Juyi (白居易), who wrote in his poem 'Li Bai's Tomb' (《李白墓》): 'Pitiful are the bones in this barren grave and exhausted spring, yet once they produced writings that startled heaven and moved the earth' (可怜荒垄穷泉骨，曾有惊天动地文). Bai Juyi used the expression to honor the sublime, world-shaking power of Li Bai's poetry. Over the centuries the phrase escaped its literary origins and came to describe any phenomenon — a battle, an invention, a speech — of extraordinary force and consequence.
example_zh: 这部电影的特效堪称惊天动地，让所有观众都为之震撼。
example_en: The special effects in this film were truly earth-shattering, leaving the entire audience in awe.

meaning: To offer a humble or modest remark in order to prompt others to share their more valuable insights or ideas. The speaker compares their own contribution to a worthless brick while hoping to elicit something as precious as jade from the audience. It is commonly used as a self-deprecating polite opener before presenting an opinion, proposal, or creative work.
origin: The idiom is attributed to the Tang dynasty poet Chang Jian (常建). Legend says Chang Jian admired the poems of his contemporary Zhao Gu (赵嘏) and devised a clever plan to obtain one. He deliberately wrote an incomplete poem on the wall of Lingyan Temple (灵岩寺), leaving the last couplet unfinished, hoping Zhao Gu would come along and fill in the missing lines. Zhao Gu eventually visited the temple, saw the poem, and indeed composed a masterful concluding couplet — far surpassing Chang Jian's verses. Thus Chang Jian's modest lines were the 'brick' and Zhao Gu's brilliant additions were the 'jade.'
example_zh: 我先谈一点粗浅的看法，算是抛砖引玉吧，希望大家畅所欲言。
example_en: Let me share a few rough thoughts first as a modest opener — I hope everyone will feel free to speak up and share their own insights.
